title: p-values, effect sizes and confidence intervals
goal: Read a result by its size and precision, not just its p-value, and tell a statistically significant effect from one that matters.

steps.title: What a p-value tells you
steps.text:
A [p-value](g:p-value) answers one narrow question: if the treatment truly did nothing, how often would chance alone give a difference at least this big? p = 0.03 means 3% of the time. By convention, p < 0.05 is called "statistically significant".

What it leaves out matters more [[c:p-not-size]]:

- how **big** the effect is
- whether it is big enough to **matter** to an athlete
- the chance that the treatment works (a common misreading)

p-values address only chance [[c:p-only-chance]]. To judge a result you also need its size and how precisely it was measured.

claims.text: A p-value can suggest whether an effect exists but does not reveal its size.

evidence.quote: While a P value can inform the reader whether an effect exists, the P value will not reveal the size of the effect.

claims.text: p-values address only chance; measures of effect with confidence intervals show strength, direction and plausible range.

evidence.quote: By contrast, p values address only chance.
Measures of association with confidence intervals reveal the strength, direction, and a plausible range of an effect as well as the likelihood of chance occurrence.

steps.title: Effect size: how big?
steps.text:
An [effect size](g:effect-size) says how big a difference is. Three common forms:

- **raw**: 9 W more mean power over a 40 km time trial
- **percent change**: 9 W on 276 W is a 3.3% gain
- **standardised**: [Cohen's d](g:cohens-d) = difference in means ÷ standard deviation (SD) between people

Cohen's rough labels: 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large [[c:cohen-labels]].

d helps compare different outcomes, but in sport the SD depends on who was studied. A mix of novices and racers has a large SD, which makes d look small. For athletes, percent change set against how much results vary from day to day is often more useful (next lesson).

claims.text: Cohen labelled standardised effect sizes of 0.2 small, 0.5 medium and 0.8 or more large.

evidence.quote: Cohen classified effect sizes as small (d = 0.2), medium (d = 0.5), and large (d ≥ 0.8).

steps.title: Cohen's d for a caffeine trial
steps.problem: In a caffeine trial, cyclists average 285 W over a 40 km time trial with caffeine and 276 W with placebo. The SD of mean power between riders is 30 W. What are Cohen's d and the percent change?
steps: Cohen's d = (mean with caffeine − mean with placebo) ÷ SD = (285 − 276) ÷ 30.
Percent change = (285 − 276) ÷ 276 × 100 = 9 ÷ 276 × 100 = 3.3%. Always divide by the starting (placebo) value.
Same result, two lenses. Which matters depends on the question: the next lesson compares changes with how much the test itself varies.

steps.title: Confidence intervals: how sure?
steps.text:
A study gives an estimate, say a 1.5% faster 10 km run. The [confidence interval](g:confidence-interval) (CI) gives the range of true effects that fit the data, for example 95% CI −0.5% to 3.5% [[c:ci-precision]].

Read it against two lines: zero, and the smallest change that matters (say 1%):

| 95% CI | reading |
|---|---|
| 1.5% to 3.5% | clearly worthwhile |
| 0.1% to 0.5% | real, but too small to matter |
| −0.5% to 3.5% | unclear: no effect to a useful one |

A wide CI means the study was too small to say much. Many sports scientists argue for judging results this way, by precision and practical importance, rather than by p < 0.05 alone [[c:precision-over-nhst]].

claims.text: Confidence intervals around an effect show how precise the result is.

evidence.quote: Confidence intervals around these measures indicate the precision of these results.

claims.text: Sports science statistical guidance recommends judging effects by the precision of their estimate rather than by null-hypothesis testing, which can't assess practical importance.

evidence.quote: using precision of estimation for inferences about population effects in preference to null-hypothesis testing, which is inadequate for assessing clinical or practical importance

steps.title: Significant isn't the same as meaningful
steps.text:
Statistical significance depends on both the size of the effect and the number of people [[c:sig-depends-n]].

- **Huge samples** make tiny effects significant [[c:huge-n-trivial]]. In 20,000 runners, a shoe that saves 0.2% over 5 km could reach p < 0.001, yet nobody would notice 3 s in a 25-minute run.
- **Small samples** miss real effects. With 8 cyclists, a true 2% gain can easily come out at p = 0.15. "Not significant" then means "not shown", not "no effect".

Sports science mostly has small samples, so the second trap is the common one. Always ask: how big, how precise, and does it matter for this athlete?

claims.text: Statistical significance depends on both sample size and effect size.

evidence.quote: Statistical significance, on the other hand, depends upon both sample size and effect size.

claims.text: Very large samples can make small, possibly trivial differences statistically significant.

evidence.quote: Huge sample sizes may detect differences that are quite small and possibly trivial.

points: A p-value is how often chance alone would give a difference this big if the treatment did nothing; it says nothing about size or importance.
Effect sizes say how big: raw units, percent change (divide by the starting value) or Cohen's d (difference ÷ SD; 0.2, 0.5, 0.8).
A confidence interval shows precision: read it against zero and against the smallest change that matters.
Huge samples make trivial effects significant; small samples miss real ones, so 'not significant' means 'not shown'.

variants.stem: A trial reports p = 0.03 for beetroot juice on 5 km run time. What does p = 0.03 mean?

options.text: With no real effect, a gap this big or bigger would occur 3% of the time
options.why: Right: the p-value is about the data, assuming no true effect.

options.text: There is a 97% chance that the juice really works
options.why: This is the most common misreading: p is not the probability that the treatment works.

options.text: The juice made the runners 3% faster on average
options.why: p says nothing about the size of the effect.

options.text: 3% of the runners in the study didn't respond
options.why: p is about the whole comparison, not individual runners.

variants.stem: A triathlon trial of a new gel reports p = 0.20 for bike split time. What does p = 0.20 mean?

options.text: With no real effect, a gap this big or bigger would occur 20% of the time
options.why: Right: the p-value is about the data, assuming no true effect.

options.text: There is only a 20% chance that the gel really works
options.why: p is not the probability that the treatment works, nor that it doesn't.

options.text: The gel made the bike split 20% faster on average
options.why: p says nothing about the size of the effect.

options.text: The gel certainly has no effect on bike split time
options.why: A large p means the data are compatible with no effect, not that there is none.

variants.stem: A study reports p < 0.001 for a new cycling training method. What important fact about the result does this p-value leave unanswered?

options.text: How big the effect is
options.why: Right: a p-value can suggest an effect exists but never reveals its size.

options.text: How surprising the data would be if the method did nothing
options.why: That is exactly what a p-value describes.

options.text: Whether chance alone easily explains the difference
options.why: A small p-value suggests chance alone is an unlikely explanation.

options.text: Which statistical test the authors ran
options.why: That is in the methods; it isn't what the p-value leaves out about the effect.

variants.stem: A running study reports an effect size of d = 0.25. By Cohen's labels, this is:

options.text: Small
options.why: Right: about 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large.

options.text: Medium
options.why: Medium is about 0.5.

options.text: Large
options.why: Large is 0.8 or more.

options.text: Too small to label
options.why: Cohen called 0.2 small, not trivial; 0.25 is above it.

variants.stem: In a 5 km run trial, runners average 1,200 s on placebo and 1,182 s on the treatment. The SD between runners is 60 s. What is Cohen's d?

options.why: Right: d = difference in means ÷ SD.
This divides the difference by the mean: a percent change, not Cohen's d.
This divides the SD by the difference: the formula upside down.
This is the raw difference; d divides it by the SD.

variants.stem: In a cycling trial, riders average 300 W on placebo and 312 W on the treatment over a 20-minute test. The SD between riders is 24 W. What is Cohen's d?

options.why: Right: d = difference in means ÷ SD.
This divides the difference by the mean: a percent change, not Cohen's d.
This divides the SD by the difference: the formula upside down.
This is the raw difference; d divides it by the SD.

variants.stem: In a triathlon swim trial, 1,500 m times average 1,320 s with the old wetsuit and 1,288 s with the new one. The SD between swimmers is 40 s. What is Cohen's d?

options.why: Right: d = difference in means ÷ SD.
This divides the difference by the mean: a percent change, not Cohen's d.
This divides the SD by the difference: the formula upside down.
This is the raw difference; d divides it by the SD.

variants.stem: After a training block, a cyclist's FTP goes from 250 W to 265 W. What is the percent change?

options.why: This divides by the new value (15 ÷ 265). Percent change uses the starting value.
15 is the change in watts, not a percentage.
This is the new value as a percentage of the old; the change is 6%.

variants.stem: A runner's 10 km time drops from 2,500 s to 2,450 s. By what percentage did the time fall?

options.why: This divides by the new value (50 ÷ 2,450). Percent change uses the starting value.
50 is the change in seconds, not a percentage.
This is the new time as a percentage of the old; the fall is 2%.

variants.stem: What does the width of a 95% confidence interval tell you?

options.text: How precisely the study pinned down the effect
options.why: Right: a narrow CI means a precise estimate; a wide one means the true effect could be quite different.

options.text: How big the effect is
options.why: The size is the point estimate in the middle; the width is the uncertainty around it.

options.text: How much athletes differ from one another
options.why: That is the SD of the sample; the CI is about the estimate of the mean effect.

options.text: The probability that the effect is real
options.why: A CI gives a range of plausible effects, not a probability that one exists.

variants.stem: The smallest change that matters to these cyclists is 1%. A study finds a 1.5% time-trial gain, 95% CI −0.5% to 3.5%. Best reading?

options.text: Clearly worthwhile: big enough to matter
options.why: The lower end is below zero, so a worthwhile benefit isn't clear.

options.text: Real, but too small to matter
options.why: The upper end is well above 1%, so 'too small to matter' isn't clear either.

options.text: Unclear: could be no effect or a useful one
options.why: Right: the interval covers no effect (and slight harm) as well as a worthwhile gain. More data are needed.

options.text: Clearly harmful: performance gets worse
options.why: Most of the interval is above zero; harm is not clear.

variants.stem: The smallest change that matters to these runners is 1%. A very large study finds a 0.3% gain in 10 km time, 95% CI 0.1% to 0.5%. Best reading?

options.text: Clearly worthwhile: big enough to matter
options.why: Even the top of the interval (0.5%) is below the 1% that matters.

options.text: Real, but too small to matter
options.why: Right: the whole interval is above zero but below 1%: a real effect, too small to matter.

options.text: Unclear: could be no effect or a useful one
options.why: The interval is narrow and excludes zero, so the effect is not unclear.

options.text: Clearly harmful: performance gets worse
options.why: The whole interval is above zero: no harm.

variants.stem: The smallest change that matters to these triathletes is 1%. A study finds a 2.5% gain in run time, 95% CI 1.5% to 3.5%. Best reading?

options.text: Clearly worthwhile: big enough to matter
options.why: Right: even the bottom of the interval (1.5%) is above the 1% that matters.

options.text: Real, but too small to matter
options.why: The whole interval is above 1%, so the effect is big enough to matter.

options.text: Unclear: could be no effect or a useful one
options.why: The interval excludes both zero and anything below 1%, so it is not unclear.

options.text: Clearly harmful: performance gets worse
options.why: The whole interval is a benefit, not harm.

variants.stem: A study of 20,000 recreational runners finds a new shoe makes 5 km times 0.2% faster, p < 0.001. How should you judge this?

options.text: Statistically significant, but probably too small to matter
options.why: Right: huge samples make tiny effects significant. 0.2% is about 3 s in 25 minutes.

options.text: A big effect, because p is so small
options.why: A small p comes from the huge sample, not from a big effect.

options.text: Unreliable, because large studies are less accurate
options.why: Large studies are more precise; the issue is that the effect is tiny.

options.text: Meaningless, because p-values should be ignored
options.why: The p-value is fine; it just answers a different question from 'does it matter?'

variants.stem: A study of 8 cyclists finds a 2.5% time-trial gain from a new warm-up, but p = 0.12. What is the best conclusion?

options.text: Not shown either way: too few riders to pin the effect down
options.why: Right: small samples miss real effects. 'Not significant' means 'not shown', and the CI likely spans zero to a large gain.

options.text: The warm-up has no effect on time-trial performance
options.why: p > 0.05 doesn't show there is no effect, only that this study couldn't rule out chance.

options.text: The warm-up works, because 2.5% is a big gain
options.why: The estimate is imprecise; with 8 riders, a 2.5% difference could easily be noise.

options.text: The study is simply wrong and should be ignored
options.why: It is weak evidence, not wrong; it can feed into a meta-analysis or a bigger trial.
